59875463.s: Juthoor and Turath Museum is one of the museums of Riyadh. It was founded by Abdulaziz Abd Rabbuh Al Hazmi, who owns a collection of heritage pieces that is good in both quantity and condition. His thinking led him to bring what he owned together in one place in an organised way, as a museum telling part of the history of Saudi Arabia. The collection covers all the elements and uses of human life in that era, made from the materials then available, such as wood, wool, leather, metal and earth, including pottery and clay vessels.
59875463.b: Juthoor and Turath Museum is one of the museums of Riyadh. It was founded by Abdulaziz Abd Rabbuh Al Hazmi, who owns a collection of heritage pieces that is good in both quantity and condition. His thinking led him to bring what he owned together in one place in an organised way, as a museum telling part of the history of Saudi Arabia. The collection covers all the elements and uses of human life in that era, made from the materials then available, such as wood, wool, leather, metal and earth, including pottery and clay vessels. There are cooking, eating and drinking vessels, as well as coffee tools, farming tools, clothing for men and women, jewellery and beauty items for women, weapons and war equipment, and more.

59786383.s: Hlewa Market is one of the most important heritage markets in Shaqra Governorate. It takes its name from an orchard next to the market called Hlewa.
59786383.b:
Hlewa Market is one of the most important heritage markets in Shaqra Governorate. It takes its name from an orchard next to the market called Hlewa.

The market was built around 1350 AH. It is large and spacious, with more than a hundred shops, and carried on varied domestic and foreign trade. It points to the commercial standing Shaqra enjoyed in the Arabian Peninsula in general. It was famous not only among the people of Shaqra but in every region, so much so that its name is no longer paired with the word "market", since what is meant is obvious. Because of its fame, this market overshadowed the markets that came before it despite being relatively recent. There is no doubt that the trade activity in it put it at the forefront of Shaqra's famous markets and was one of the reasons their activity declined, and even disappeared, once it took the lead. This was not only because it had more shops or a larger area, but because its rise brought the dominance of retail trade and the large number of products on display, and a decline in the wholesale trade that Shaqra's merchants had controlled in the days of the earlier markets, which dealt only in simple, local retail. It sold household supplies, tools and utensils, vegetables, fruit, local products and sheep, and other services were located next to it, such as a flour mill, a crop-selling area and the public scale (al-qabban).

59786272.s: Harmah (pronounced with an a on the Ha, a silent Ra, and an a on the Mim, ending in ta marbuta) lies about 195 kilometres north-west of the city of Riyadh, at longitude 45.3406 east and latitude 25.9233 north. It is embraced by Wadi Al Batin, where Wadi Al Kalb and Wadi Al Mushaqqar meet, joining in the lake of Harmah Dam. Harmah shares Wadi Al Kalb with the city of Al Majmaah, as is well known, but depends on the floods of these two valleys, which come together in this large dam, about 400 metres long, built of stone by the people of Harmah hundreds of years ago.
59786272.b: Harmah (pronounced with an a on the Ha, a silent Ra, and an a on the Mim, ending in ta marbuta) lies about 195 kilometres north-west of the city of Riyadh, at longitude 45.3406 east and latitude 25.9233 north. It is embraced by Wadi Al Batin, where Wadi Al Kalb and Wadi Al Mushaqqar meet, joining in the lake of Harmah Dam. Harmah shares Wadi Al Kalb with the city of Al Majmaah, as is well known, but depends on the floods of these two valleys, which come together in this large dam, about 400 metres long, built of stone by the people of Harmah hundreds of years ago. The Ministry of Agriculture later reinforced it and regulated the discharge of its floodwater through artificial channels to Harmah's farms, and whatever flood water exceeds Harmah's needs goes east along the course of Wadi Al Batin. Some of Harmah's farms and palm groves lie south of this valley: Al Dhahiriyah, Saat Allah, Al Wusta and Qilban Al Ood, and south of the valley also lie Muraiqib Ibn Duraiys and Dhahrat Mushrifah. The valley separates the town of Harmah from the town of Al Majmaah, and descends with the flood until it reaches Riyadh Subha, Al Khufaisah, Mutribah and others, cutting through the Al Mijzal ridge through the Al Kathima opening.

59786204.s: Jalajil was one of the strongest towns of Sudair in the eleventh century AH. It was named after the jaljalah of water, the murmur of water as it moves between the rocks of the valleys. Jalajil is known for its many palm trees and large date production, and it also has some historic places such as the watchtower, the old mosque, the Emirate Palace and the palace of Suwaid bin Ali.

59786195.s: The Abdullah bin Mohammed Abu Batin Heritage Museum is a heritage museum on Abdullah bin Mohammed Abu Batin's farm, "Al Aidiyah", in Raudat Sudair. Prince Ahmed bin Abdulaziz opened the museum on 13/02/1436 AH. It holds more than 5,000 heritage pieces that portray the life of the Sudair region in the past, in terms of its professional, craft and farming work, as well as manuscripts, coins, traditional weapons and maps.

59786144.s: Awdat Sudair is known for its fertile land and many valleys, which has led to thriving farming and wide pastures. Its people depend first of all on agriculture, and farmers produce the finest types of wheat, corn and barley. They also take great care of palm trees and produce many kinds of dates, such as Khudhari, Muqfazi, Dukhaini, Halwa, Saqai, Maskani and Sawdi. The village depends on the floods that run in Wadi Sudair, known to the townspeople as Al Baten: when this valley flows, the wells fill with water and the palms are irrigated.
59786144.b:
Awdat Sudair is known for its fertile land and many valleys, which has led to thriving farming and wide pastures. Its people depend first of all on agriculture, and farmers produce the finest types of wheat, corn and barley. They also take great care of palm trees and produce many kinds of dates, such as Khudhari, Muqfazi, Dukhaini, Halwa, Saqai, Maskani and Sawdi. The village depends on the floods that run in Wadi Sudair, known to the townspeople as Al Baten: when this valley flows, the wells fill with water and the palms are irrigated. Several other valleys also contribute, such as Wadi Al Jawfa, which irrigates the upper part of the town; Wadi Al Shuaba, which irrigates the lower part of the town; and Wadi Al Dakhila, which irrigates the lower part of the town and Sanaa south of the town (the private flood channel), which irrigates the farms and palace of the Al Eissa family.

Social life in Awdat Sudair reflects the traditions and heritage of the people of Najd. The Najdi Ardah has been passed down there since ancient times, and the people are keen to perform it on happy occasions, especially on Eid day. Among the folk arts loved by poetry lovers are the harvest song, sung by farmers especially among the wheat ears, and the poetry art known as al-radd, along with popular poetry.

Signs of renewal and development have reached Awdat Sudair as they have the Kingdom's other cities and villages, with modern housing, commercial institutions, and educational and health facilities built there and provided with all public utilities and services.

There are also places and antiquities found there by the Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage, and there are sources saying that these antiquities date from before Islam.
59786144.a: Al Awdah, Al Majmaah, Riyadh Province

59785976.s: The people of Ash Shu'ara centre, part of Dawadmi Governorate, have revived the history of the old houses, mosque and shops by restoring them and turning them into a tourist village, with gates built on all sides because of their historical importance and in line with the efforts of the Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage to develop heritage villages. The village has witnessed important historical events, including the battle of the people of Ash Shu'ara with the Ashraf in 1205 AH (1791), the Battle of Sufah in 1319 AH (1901), and the Ash Shu'ara Conference, called by King Abdulaziz, may God have mercy on him, and held on Thursday 1/5/1348 AH.

59785974.t: King Abdulaziz Historic Palace in Dawadmi
59785974.s: King Abdulaziz Palace is an archaeological palace owned by King Abdulaziz bin Abdulrahman Al Saud. It lies on the western side of Dawadmi Governorate along the Hijaz road and is notable for its beautiful building on a large site. The early stages of founding the palace began in 1349 AH, when King Abdulaziz ordered Sheikh Abdulrahman Abu Bakr Al Ghaihab to choose a suitable site for building a palace for the king in Dawadmi.
59785974.b:
King Abdulaziz Palace is an archaeological palace owned by King Abdulaziz bin Abdulrahman Al Saud. It lies on the western side of Dawadmi Governorate along the Hijaz road and is notable for its beautiful building on a large site. The early stages of founding the palace began in 1349 AH, when King Abdulaziz ordered Sheikh Abdulrahman Abu Bakr Al Ghaihab to choose a suitable site for building a palace for the king in Dawadmi.

King Abdulaziz Palace in Dawadmi Governorate consists of a number of buildings, the most prominent being the royal wing, which includes the royal residence with its facilities, the roshan (the king's private majlis), the workshops for repairing royal cars, and the mashab, which was used to prepare coffee, tea and other amenities.

The palace received great attention from the Ministry of Education's Deputy Ministry for Antiquities and Museums (formerly), which carried out a project to restore this archaeological palace under the supervision of the Boys' Education Department in Dawadmi Governorate, represented by the department's Museums and Antiquities section. The project tender was awarded to the Bawabat Al Jazeera company, which specialises in restoring antiquities and museums, for SAR 4.6 million.
59785974.a: King Abdulaziz Archaeological Palace, Al Duwadimi, Dawadmi

59785929.s: King Abdulaziz Palace is one of the historic archaeological palaces in Al-Kharj Governorate, specifically in the city of Al Sayh, the former capital of Al-Kharj, and it still stands today. It was built in 1359 AH (1940) by order of King Abdulaziz Al Saud, to protect Riyadh and its southern borders from any rebellion against the state. It was built in Al-Kharj specifically because it was a strategic target for anyone wishing to control Al Yamamah and Najd in that era. Al-Kharj is distinguished by its natural resources, its fertile land and its abundant springs.
59785929.b: King Abdulaziz Palace is one of the historic archaeological palaces in Al-Kharj Governorate, specifically in the city of Al Sayh, the former capital of Al-Kharj, and it still stands today. It was built in 1359 AH (1940) by order of King Abdulaziz Al Saud, to protect Riyadh and its southern borders from any rebellion against the state. It was built in Al-Kharj specifically because it was a strategic target for anyone wishing to control Al Yamamah and Najd in that era. Al-Kharj is distinguished by its natural resources, its fertile land and its abundant springs, and it has many important archaeological sites, some dating back to 500 BC, such as the ancient burial grounds and the Al Binnah archaeological sites in Al Yamamah, which caravans passed through on their journey from the Levant to Yemen and back, known as the winter and summer journey.
59785929.a: King Faisal Road, Al Aziziyyah, Al-Kharj

59785926.s: Qasr Al Sharia Archaeological Mosque is one of the most prominent archaeological buildings in Riyadh Region, notable for its construction of mud and stone in the Najdi style.
59785926.b:
Qasr Al Sharia Archaeological Mosque is one of the most prominent archaeological buildings in Riyadh Region, notable for its construction of mud and stone in the Najdi style.

Beyond being a place of worship, it is also a cultural beacon for learning, where many lessons and lectures are held.

59785924.t: Al Musa Museum in Al Sulaymiyah
59785924.s: Saleh bin Ibrahim Al Musa Museum is one of the museums of Riyadh Region, in the town of Al Sulaymiyah in Al-Kharj Governorate. It was founded by Saleh bin Ibrahim Al Musa. The museum has 5 halls, and its contents are displayed in several ways: some inside cabinets or display cases, some on shelves, and some hung on the walls.
59785924.b:
Saleh bin Ibrahim Al Musa Museum is one of the museums of Riyadh Region, in the town of Al Sulaymiyah in Al-Kharj Governorate. It was founded by Saleh bin Ibrahim Al Musa. The museum has 5 halls, and its contents are displayed in several ways: some inside cabinets or display cases, some on shelves, and some hung on the walls. The exhibits in the halls are as follows:

First hall: palm-leaf crafts, leather goods and some metal vessels.

Second hall: a collection of old radios and gramophones.

Third hall: an exhibition of photographs of old cars.

Fourth hall: a reception hall with a projector.

Fifth hall: the main hall, which holds a large collection of heritage items.

59785921.s: King Abdulaziz Historic Arish in the town of Al Sulaymiyah is one of the most important historic landmarks, overseen by the Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage, and was recently included in the Kingdom's tourist trails project. The arish's historical importance lies in its link to the founder, King Abdulaziz, may God have mercy on him, who used it as his majlis on his visits to Al-Kharj Governorate.
